This picks up where [Get Started](MitoPilot.html) left off: the test project is
set up and the app is open on the Assemble module. Assemble cleans the reads,
builds mitogenome assemblies, maps the reads back to measure coverage, and
BLASTs each assembly against GenBank to find its closest published relative.

## Set the options

Every processing step has an options set, shown as a link in the sample table.
Click the `default` link in the **Assembly Opts.** column to see what the
assembler will do.

![Assembly options window](figures/get-started/assemble-opts.png)

Nothing is editable until you tick **Edit**. The important controls:

- **CPUs and Memory** per sample. Raise memory if samples fail with out-of-memory
  errors.
- **Assembler.** [GetOrganelle](https://github.com/Kinggerm/GetOrganelle) by
  default, or [MitoFinder](https://github.com/RemiAllio/MitoFinder). GetOrganelle
  only assembles reads it recognises as mitochondrial, which makes it fast but
  dependent on good reference databases. MitoFinder assembles everything, which
  is much slower but can work better for groups with few reference mitogenomes.
- **Seeds and Labels databases.** The reference sequences GetOrganelle uses to
  recruit and extend mitochondrial reads. The defaults are fish; for other
  groups, build your own with `custom_assembly_db()` (see
  [custom databases](custom_dbs.html)).
- **Max assembly paths / Max scaffolds.** Samples that come apart into more
  pieces than this are marked failed instead of continuing.
- **Automatically join multi-scaffold assemblies.** Off by default, and worth
  leaving off until you understand your data. See
  [multiple paths and scaffolds](Multiple-Assemblies.html).

Options are saved as named, reusable sets. To make one, tick **Edit**, change
what you want, type a new name in the **Parameter set name** box, and click
**Update**. That name then appears in the dropdown for any sample. Different
samples can use different sets, which is how you give the difficult ones more
memory without paying for it everywhere.

For the test project the defaults are fine.

## Run the workflow

Click **UPDATE** at the top of the window. MitoPilot shows the Nextflow command
it is about to run and how many samples it applies to.

![Update window showing the Nextflow command and Run from App button](figures/get-started/update-window.png)

**Run from App** runs the pipeline in your R session. The Progress window
updates as samples move through the steps, and the spinning gears in the corner
mean work is still happening. This is the simplest option, and the right one for
a project this size.

<div class="alert alert-warning">
<strong>Watch out.</strong> Running from the app ties the pipeline to the app
session. For large projects, or anything on a cluster, save or submit a job
script instead so the run survives a dropped connection. See
<a href="Custom-HPC.html">HPC cluster support</a>.
</div>

Assemble runs three steps per sample: read pre-processing with
[fastp](https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp), assembly with GetOrganelle, and
read mapping with [bowtie2](https://github.com/BenLangmead/bowtie2) to compute
depth and error rates. It then BLASTs each assembly against GenBank and fetches
the best-matching reference, which is the slowest part because it waits on NCBI.
Nextflow runs samples in parallel, so the whole test project takes a while but
not fifteen times one sample.

Failures are normal and mostly mean a sample ran out of memory; MitoPilot retries
those with more. Common errors are covered in the
[FAQ](FAQ.html) and [troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.html) articles.

## Read the results

When the run finishes, the table fills in.

![MitoPilot sample table in the Assemble module](figures/get-started/assemble-table.png)

Useful columns: **Reads** surviving pre-processing, **Topology** (circular or
linear), **Asmb. Length**, and **# Paths** / **# Scaffolds**, which tell you
whether the sample came back as one clean sequence or something messier. The
BLAST columns name the closest GenBank record.

`output` opens the sample's results folder. `details` opens the assembly itself.

### Coverage and error

In the details window, `view` opens a plot of read depth, error rate, and GC
content along the assembly.

![Read depth, error rate, and GC content along an assembly](figures/get-started/coverage-plot.png)

This is SRR21843972 (*Stomias affinis*). Depth collapses at both ends, which is
why the assembly came back linear rather than circular: there were not enough
reads spanning that region to close the circle. Options are more sequencing,
different GetOrganelle settings, or accepting a partial genome.

## The awkward samples

Three test samples are deliberately awkward, and between them they cover most of
what goes wrong with real data.

### Not enough data

SRR22396758 (*Upeneus parvus*) carries a warning icon and the note
"Insufficient sequencing depth". Its read file was truncated to 200 reads on
purpose. The threshold is the `min_depth` argument at project setup. There is
nothing to fix here, so leave this sample behind when you lock the rest.

### Two competing assemblies

SRR21844202 (*Fundulus majalis*) is flagged "Unable to resolve single assembly
from reads": GetOrganelle found two valid paths through a tangled assembly graph.
Open `details` and you see both, each 19,332 bp.

Select both and click **Align**.

![Alignment of two competing assembly paths with a conflict block highlighted](figures/get-started/multipath-align.png)

The paths are 99.99% identical, disagreeing at two single-base positions.
MitoPilot classifies each conflict, here "Likely heteroplasmy / SNP", and shows
read depth and error rate around it so you can see whether both alleles have real
support.

From here you can:

- **Ignore the extras.** Click the ignore control on the paths you do not want.
  Only what remains goes to annotation. This is what we do for the test project.
- **Build a resolved assembly.** Choose how to handle each conflict block and
  MitoPilot writes a single reconciled sequence as **Path 0**, superseding the
  alternatives.

![Assembly details with the second path marked ignored](figures/get-started/multipath-ignored.png)

<div class="alert alert-note">
<strong>Note.</strong> Recording both alleles with IUPAC ambiguity codes is
available, but MITOS2 handles ambiguous bases poorly at the annotation step, so
prefer picking an allele unless the heteroplasmy is the point of your study.
</div>

### Fragmented assemblies

Two samples come back in pieces, and they need opposite treatment. This is the
distinction that matters most, so it is worth doing both.

**SCAFFJOIN** (*Conger oceanicus*) is one mitogenome broken into three
scaffolds. Open its details and MitoPilot shows the scaffold join editor.

![Scaffold join editor showing three scaffolds mapped to one reference](figures/get-started/scaffjoin-join-editor.png)

All three scaffolds map to the same reference (NC_083079.1) at 100% coverage,
and the plot lays them out along it: scaffold 1 reversed, then scaffolds 2 and 3,
with gaps between them. That is exactly the signature of one genome that the
assembler could not connect. You can override the order or orientation, tick
**Circular** if appropriate, and then click **Build joined assembly (Path 0)**.

![Assembly details after building the joined Path 0](figures/get-started/scaffjoin-joined.png)

The joined Path 0 is 17,652 bp, the three original scaffolds are marked ignored,
and the sample is locked automatically. The note records how it was built,
including how many N bases fill the gaps. Those Ns are real missing sequence, and
MitoPilot warns you about them because MITOS2 does not handle ambiguous bases
well.

**MULTISCAFF** looks superficially similar, two scaffolds in one path, but it is
the opposite case.

![Warning that scaffolds map to different references](figures/get-started/multiscaff-details.png)

MitoPilot refuses to go quietly here: the scaffolds carry *different* BLAST hits,
and the mapping plot shows the second one only sparsely aligned (hatched) to the
reference. These are two different animals, from contamination or a mixed sample.
Joining them would fabricate a chimeric genome. Leave them separate, and each is
annotated, validated, and exported as its own record.

<div class="alert alert-tip">
<strong>Tip.</strong> Fragmented does not automatically mean joinable. Check that
the pieces map to the same reference, in a sensible order, without overlapping
each other, before you join anything. Contamination, NUMTs, and naturally
multipartite mitogenomes all look like "extra scaffolds" at first glance.
</div>

## Lock and move on

Select every sample that assembled successfully, which is all of them except
SRR22396758, and click **LOCK**.

![Sample table with successful samples selected for locking](figures/get-started/assemble-selected.png)

Locking freezes those samples in Assemble and releases them to the Annotate
module. Then switch modules with the dropdown at the top left and carry on with
[annotation](Test-Project-Annotate.html).
